sentences.text: Microcleidus possessed forty neck vertebrae and a short tail containing twenty-eight vertebrae.
The animal is known from well-preserved fossils, including a nearly complete skeleton featuring a neck longer than that of contemporary plesiosaurs.
Its anatomy included unusually long, tiny anterior cervical vertebrae and a clavicle reduced to a thin leaf attached to the dorsal surface of the anterior shoulder bone branches.
The interclavicular space in this creature was practically non-existent.
The type species M. homalospondylus was the largest known, reaching 5.1 meters in length and weighing 650 kilograms.
Other species were smaller, with M. tournemirensis measuring about 4 meters and 300 kilograms, and M. melusinae measuring about 3 meters and 120 kilograms.
Richard Owen described the type species Plesiosaurus homalospondylus in 1865 based on a skeleton lacking the lower body, which was later exhibited at the British Museum in London.
Watson recognized the characteristic reduced clavicles in another P. homalospondylus skeleton in 1909 and subsequently described the new genus Microcleidus, meaning small clavicle.
Watson classified P. macropterus into the same genus two years later as a distinct species, differentiating it based on large rear flippers.
Microcleidus belongs to the family Plesiosauridae.
In 2004, Ketchum and Benson determined that Microcleidus belonged to the family Plesiosauridae alongside Seeleyosaurus, Hydrorion, Occitanosaurus, and Plesiosaurus.
Microcleidus was later considered the most primitive and oldest member of the elasmosaurids, a group of plesiosaurs with exceptionally long necks that spread during the Cretaceous.
Among these relatives, the closest relative is Occitanosaurus, which however possesses large clavicles.
Fossils of the genus have been found in France, the Posidonia Shale in Germany and Luxembourg, and the Alum Shale Formation of England.
This plesiosaur lived in the Early Jurassic (Toarcian, about 190 million years ago), with fossils recovered in England.
Microcleidus lived during the Toarcian stage, between 184.2 and 174.7 million years ago.
Some researchers consider Microcleidus to be one of the oldest elasmosaurids.
